transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you in today?

I guess what finally made me come in is… my eating has felt really out of control sometimes. Like after a really long day on site, or if I’ve been at a neighborhood meeting and I’m already kind of wound up and tired, I’ll get home and just start eating way more than I meant to.

It’s not like I sit down planning some huge meal. It’s more like I’ll have leftover takeout, then maybe cereal, then chips, whatever is around, and I keep going even when I’m past full. By the end I’m uncomfortably full and kind of embarrassed, honestly. It’s been bothering me enough that I thought I should actually talk to someone instead of just telling myself I’ll handle it better next week.
After these episodes of overeating, do you ever try to compensate by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising a lot more than usual?

Yeah… I have. Not every time, but a few times a month after those nights, I’ll go into the bathroom and make myself throw up. I feel awful saying that out loud.

It’s usually when I’m already panicking, like I can’t stop thinking, “I just ruined everything,” because I put so much effort into looking put-together and keeping myself presentable at work and in meetings. And then after eating like that, I get this frantic feeling that I need to undo it somehow. So… yes, I’ve made myself vomit.
How often would you say you’ve made yourself vomit after these episodes of overeating — is it happening at least once a week, or more frequently than that?

If I’m being honest, looking back over the last few months, it’s probably averaged out to about once a week. It’s not perfectly regular, though. Like, there are some weeks where it happens twice, especially if I’ve had a couple really stressful evenings back-to-back, and then there might be a week where I don’t do it at all and I tell myself, “Okay, maybe I’m getting a handle on this.”

But when I step back and actually count it instead of just minimizing it… yeah, it’s been roughly weekly. Which feels hard to admit, because in my head I kept thinking of it as “just sometimes,” but I guess “sometimes” has been more often than I wanted to acknowledge.

When you’re having these episodes and making yourself vomit afterward, is it mainly because you feel you’ve lost control over your eating, or is it more because you’re worried about gaining weight or how your body looks?

It’s… honestly both, but if I’m really being truthful, the body and weight piece is a big part of what makes it feel so urgent afterward.

Like, yes, during the eating part I feel out of control, and that’s scary. But the panic after is usually more like, “Now I’m going to look different,” or, “People are going to notice.” Since I started wearing more fitted work clothes and being up front more at meetings, I catch myself judging almost the whole day by whether my pants feel tight or whether I think people can see my stomach.

It sounds kind of ridiculous when I say it, because I know people are probably focused on the project or whatever we’re discussing, not staring at me. But in my head it becomes this huge thing. If my clothes feel snug, I feel like I’ve failed somehow, and then after I eat too much, it’s like I’m desperate to undo it so I don’t have to sit with that feeling the next day.
Do you judge or evaluate yourself more harshly based on your body shape or weight than you think is reasonable?

Yes… I do. More than I want to admit.

It’s like, since I started wearing more fitted work clothes and having to be more visible in meetings, I can’t just get dressed and move on with my day. I’ll notice whether my pants feel tight, or I’ll sit there wondering if people can see my stomach when I’m standing up in front of everyone. And then that can kind of color the whole day for me.

Like, if I feel okay in my clothes, I feel more confident, more in control. But if something feels snug or I think I look bigger, I get really self-conscious and harsh with myself, like I’ve done something wrong. I know, logically, that it probably isn’t reasonable and that other people aren’t paying that much attention. But in the moment it feels really important, almost like my whole sense of whether I’m doing well depends on it.
Would you say that your feelings about yourself are overly influenced by your body shape or weight, more so than you think is reasonable?

Yes… I think that’s probably true. I don’t like saying it that bluntly, but yeah, my opinion of myself can swing way too much based on how I think I look that day.

Since I started wearing more fitted work clothes and being more up front in meetings, it’s gotten harder to ignore. I’ll be getting dressed and if my pants feel even a little tight, it can set the tone for the whole day. Or if I’m standing in front of people, I’ll suddenly be thinking, “Can they see my stomach? Do I look bigger?” instead of just focusing on what I’m supposed to be saying.

And I know, rationally, that’s probably not what anyone else is thinking about. But in my head it becomes this measure of whether I’m okay or not that day. If I feel like I look acceptable, I feel more confident and like I can handle things. If I don’t, I get really self-critical, like I’ve somehow failed. So yes, I’d say it influences how I feel about myself more than is reasonable.
Has your sense of self-worth been strongly affected by your concerns about your weight or body shape, more than you feel is reasonable?

Yes… yeah, I think it has. More than it should.

I feel a little embarrassed saying that because I know my worth shouldn’t depend on something like whether my pants feel tight, but lately it kind of does, at least in my head. Since I started wearing more fitted work clothes and being up front more in meetings, I’m just so aware of my body all the time. Like I’ll be standing there trying to talk about work, and part of my brain is focused on whether people can see my stomach or whether I look bigger than I did before.

And if I feel like my clothes fit okay, I can almost relax and feel like I’m doing fine as a person, which sounds dramatic, but that’s how it feels. But if they feel snug, it can ruin the whole day for me. I start judging myself really harshly, like I’ve failed somehow, even if nothing else has gone wrong. So yes, I’d say my self-worth gets wrapped up in my weight and shape in a way that I know isn’t reasonable.

When you’ve made yourself vomit after eating, does it feel more like you’re doing it because you’re afraid of gaining weight or changing how your body looks, or more because you feel you’ve lost control and need to ‘reset’ somehow?

It’s… probably more about the fear of gaining weight or my body looking different, if I’m being honest. There’s definitely a “reset” feeling too, but the panic that comes first is usually about feeling like I’ve undone everything.

Like after those nights where I’ve eaten more than I meant to, or I feel really full, I’ll start thinking about how hard I’ve been trying to look put-together, especially at work. And then I get this rush of panic like, “Now it’s going to show, now my clothes are going to feel tight, now I’m going to look bigger.” It’s not every day or anything, but a few times a month after nights like that, I’ve gone into the bathroom and made myself throw up.

I hate saying that out loud. But in the moment it feels like I need to fix it quickly, before it turns into something visible on my body. So yes, it’s tied to feeling out of control, but mostly the fear is about undoing all the work I’ve put into looking okay.
Do you find that your concerns about your weight or body shape affect your sense of self-worth or how you evaluate yourself on a daily basis?

Yes, it does. I mean, I know I kind of already said that, but it really does show up day to day.

Since I started wearing more fitted clothes for work and being more visible in meetings, I feel like I’m constantly checking myself in my head. Like, if I put on pants in the morning and they feel tight, even a little, I’ll take that as a sign the whole day is going to be bad, or that I look wrong somehow. And then I’m distracted, because instead of thinking about what I’m saying or doing, I’m wondering if people can see my stomach or if I look bigger than I did before.

It’s embarrassing because it sounds so small when I say it out loud, like “my pants felt tight,” but in the moment it feels like this huge judgment about me as a person. If I feel okay in my clothes, I feel more competent and comfortable. If I don’t, I get really down on myself, like I’ve failed before the day even starts. So yes, my weight and shape definitely affect how I evaluate myself, probably way more than they should.
Do you ever judge yourself as a person—like whether you're good or bad, capable or not—based on your weight or how you look?

Yes… I do. I don’t like admitting that, because it sounds so shallow when I say it plainly, but that is what happens in my head.

Since I started wearing more fitted work clothes and being up front in meetings more, I catch myself sort of measuring the whole day by how my body feels in my clothes. Like if my pants feel tight in the morning, I don’t just think, “Oh, these pants are uncomfortable.” I immediately start thinking I look bad, or I’ve let myself go, or people are going to notice my stomach when I’m standing there talking. And then somehow that turns into me feeling less capable, like I’m not presenting myself well enough or I don’t have it together.

It’s not even always based on anything real anyone has said. It’s more like I decide, based on how I look or how I think I look, whether I’m doing okay as a person that day. If I feel like I look fine, I can be more confident. But if I feel bigger or exposed or like my stomach is noticeable, I get really hard on myself, like I’ve failed before anything has even happened. So yes, I do judge myself that way, more than I want to.
Have these concerns about your weight or body shape caused you significant distress or affected your ability to function in your daily life, such as at work or in social situations?

Yes, I think it has, even though I’m still functioning on the surface. Like, I’m still going to work, I’m still doing my job, I’m not missing meetings or anything obvious like that. From the outside I probably look like I’m handling things normally.

But it’s started affecting what I do around work, especially after meetings or long days. If people say, “Let’s grab food after,” or there’s some casual thing where everyone’s going to eat, I’ve been turning those down more. I’ll make excuses like I’m tired or I have something to do at home, but really it’s because I’m worried that once I’m there, the evening will get away from me. Like I’ll eat more than I planned, or I’ll feel too full, and then I’ll spend the whole night panicking about it.

Sometimes I’ll just rush home instead of hanging around, even if part of me wants to go and be normal with everyone. It’s not like I’ve stopped living my life completely, but it does feel like my choices are getting smaller. I’m planning around the fear of how I’ll feel in my body afterward, instead of just deciding based on whether I actually want to go. So yes, it’s causing distress, and it’s starting to interfere socially, especially connected to work.

And then somehow that turns into me feeling less capable, like I’m not presenting myself well enough or I don’t have it together.

It’s not even always based on anything real anyone has said. It’s more like I decide, based on how I look or how I think I look, whether I’m doing okay as a person that day. If I feel like I look fine, I can be more confident. But if I feel bigger or exposed or like my stomach is noticeable, I get really hard on myself, like I’ve failed before anything has even happened. So yes, I do judge myself that way, more than I want to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's self-evaluation is influenced by concerns about shape or weight to the extent that it interferes with daily functioning or causes significant distress, which would support a diagnosis of bulimia nervosa (F50.2) over an unspecified eating disorder (F50.8).
doctor.question: Have these concerns about your weight or body shape caused you significant distress or affected your ability to function in your daily life, such as at work or in social situations?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up and doing my job, but I’ve started turning down some after-meeting food plans or rushing home because I’m worried the evening will get away from me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the weight/body-shape concerns have caused distress or interfered with daily functioning, especially work or social situations.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think it has, even though I’m still functioning on the surface. Like, I’m still going to work, I’m still doing my job, I’m not missing meetings or anything obvious like that. From the outside I probably look like I’m handling things normally.

But it’s started affecting what I do around work, especially after meetings or long days. If people say, “Let’s grab food after,” or there’s some casual thing where everyone’s going to eat, I’ve been turning those down more. I’ll make excuses like I’m tired or I have something to do at home, but really it’s because I’m worried that once I’m there, the evening will get away from me. Like I’ll eat more than I planned, or I’ll feel too full, and then I’ll spend the whole night panicking about it.

Sometimes I’ll just rush home instead of hanging around, even if part of me wants to go and be normal with everyone. It’s not like I’ve stopped living my life completely, but it does feel like my choices are getting smaller. I’m planning around the fear of how I’ll feel in my body afterward, instead of just deciding based on whether I actually want to go. So yes, it’s causing distress, and it’s starting to interfere socially, especially connected to work.

inference.note: The patient meets criteria for bulimia nervosa, including recurrent episodes of binge eating, recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors (e.g., self-induced vomiting), and undue influence of body shape and weight on self-evaluation, occurring at least once a week for several months. No evidence supports an alternative diagnosis in the differential at this time.
